summary: We developed an interactive game about space missions for children ages 7 to 12, based on the idea of what you have to do to successfully complete the game and survive the 10 days of the mission. We approached the challenge creatively, aiming for children to simulate the reality of a space mission. It is important because, besides showing what it would be like, it helps thousands of children learn more about space, explore their curiosity, and plant the seed of knowledge so that in the future, if they wish, they can steer their career or trade toward these topics.
details: Mission: Last Refuge is an educational video game for children ages 7 to 12 that runs in a web browser. The player is the commander of a base at the Moon’s south pole and must keep it running throughout the mission by managing three resources: oxygen, energy, and protection against radiation. Each day brings a new situation, such as a solar alert, a long lunar night, or an outside repair, with two or three options that show in advance which resources they use up or improve. After each decision, the game updates the resources and explains the result, and the mission succeeds only if oxygen and energy end above zero and protection reaches at least 20 points. The project lets children experience a space mission without leaving home, sparks curiosity, and offers brief, accessible information about space exploration, while children learn by doing that every decision has a benefit and a cost, which strengthens critical thinking and responsible decision-making. We hope millions of children will play it and fall in love with space and science, and since it is free and works in any browser, schools and families can use it easily. We developed it with HTML for the structure, CSS for the look, and JavaScript for the game logic, in a single file that opens in Chrome, Edge, or Firefox on any computer with no installation needed. We relied on open-source code and on artificial intelligence tools such as Gemini and Claude, since we are still learning to program, and we drew inspiration from open NASA sources such as DONKI (space weather), OSDR (biological research in space), and the Artemis program. Its creativity lies in the fact that the story is not fixed: the player’s decisions determine whether the mission succeeds or fails, so every game can be different, and it also turns real space problems, such as solar storms and limited energy, into a retro pixel-art game that appeals to children. As a team, we took into account the age of the audience, with simple language and clear visuals; free access with no installation; learning through short explanations after each result; scientific honesty, by making clear that the game’s numbers are simulated even though its topics are based on NASA; and future improvements, for which the code includes an editable settings section that will make it possible to add days, a Mars scenario, and real solar events.
